Empirical Research Plan: Wrongful-Discharge Laws and the Rise of Temporary Help Employment, 1979-1995
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy
   • Difference-in-Differences with Staggered Adoption (event-study implementation).  
   • Justification
     – Each state adopts the three wrongful-discharge doctrines in different calendar years, generating plausibly exogenous policy variation.  
     – Monthly CPS and quarterly QCEW provide long pretreatment and post-treatment panels.  
     – A two-way-fixed-effects (TWFE) DID would be biased under heterogeneous effects (Goodman-Bacon 2021). Therefore we implement an estimator designed for staggered timing (Sun & Abraham 2021 or Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021) and show dynamic event-time coefficients.  

2. Treatment and Control
   • Treatment variable  
     Main specification: ImpliedContract_s,t = 1 after state s first recognizes the implied-contract exception (0 otherwise).  
     Extensions: (a) separate dummies for each doctrine; (b) cumulative‐count (0-3) measuring breadth of protection.  
   • Control group  
     – For a given event-time coefficient k, states that have not yet adopted by t serve as controls (“not-yet-treated” comparison).  
     – After adoption, a state remains treated; it never re-enters the control pool.  
   • Treatment timing  
     – Event date = first month the doctrine is legally effective (statutory effective date or date of landmark court decision).  
     – CPS monthly data: we set Treatment=1 beginning in the month of adoption; QCEW quarterly uses quarter of adoption.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
   A1. Parallel Trends: Absent adoption, treated and comparison states would have evolved similarly in temporary-help intensity.  
       Plausibility: no national push for temp agencies aimed only at soon-to-adopt states; we will test pre-trends.  
   A2. No Anticipation: Firms do not increase temp-agency use before the legal doctrine is actually in place (can be evaluated via leads).  
       Plausibility: court decisions are difficult to predict; statutory adoptions sometimes anticipated → check for pre-effects.  
   A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-state spillovers): A doctrine in state s does not alter temp-help use in neighboring untreated states.  
       Plausibility: agencies operate locally; large multi-state clients could partially violate this → border-county robustness.  
   A4. Composition Stability: Adoption does not systematically change which workers/industries are sampled in CPS within a state-year cell.  
       Plausibility: CPS sampling frame fixed; migration flows small relative to workforce.  
   A5. Exogenous Timing Conditional on Controls: After conditioning on state FE, year×month FE, and observables (unemployment, unionization, etc.), the exact year of adoption is as-good-as-random.  
       Plausibility: Legal evolution often triggered by idiosyncratic court cases rather than macro conditions, but we will control and test.  

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
   1. Endogenous Adoption (policy follows labor-market distress).  
      – Include state-specific linear trends and time-varying covariates.  
      – Event-study pre-trend test; drop states that show strong differential pre-trends.  
      – Instrument timing with political variables (e.g., partisan composition of state supreme court) as robustness.  
   2. Contemporaneous Labor Policies (e.g., minimum-wage hikes, workers’-comp reforms).  
      – Control for a vector of other policy dummies.  
      – Triple-difference: compare temp-help industries to similar low-skill service industries inside the same state×month.  
   3. Spillovers through Multi-State Firms/Agencies.  
      – Border-pair specification: compare counties adjacent across treated/untreated borders.  
      – Include region×time FE to soak up any regional diffusion of temp-help business models.  

5. R Code Outline (executable)

```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)       # fast data
library(fixest)           # feols with Sun & Abraham
library(did)              # Callaway & Sant'Anna estimator
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load CPS micro sample (assumed csv already cleaned to 1979-1995)
cps <- fread("cps_79_95.csv")

# 2. Load wrongful-discharge adoption dates
wd_dates <- fread("wd_adoption_dates.csv")   # columns: state, doctrine, adopt_date (YYYY-MM)

# 3. Merge and construct treatment
cps[, date := as.IDate(paste(year, month, "01", sep="-"))]
wd_implied <- wd_dates[doctrine=="implied_contract"][, .(state, adopt_date)]
cps <- merge(cps, wd_implied, by="state", all.x=TRUE)

cps[, treated := ( !is.na(adopt_date) & date >= adopt_date ) ]
cps[, g := year(adopt_date)]                       # cohort year
cps[, t := year(date)]                            # calendar year (for C&S estimator)
cps[, id := .I]                                   # individual id

# 4. Outcome: employed in temp help services
cps[, temphelp := (empstat=="Employed" & (sic==7362 | naics==56132))]
# Collapse to state-month cell to speed
cell <- cps[, .(
    temp_share = mean(temphelp, na.rm=TRUE),
    unem = mean(unemployed, na.rm=TRUE),
    manuf = mean(manufact, na.rm=TRUE),
    union = mean(union_member, na.rm=TRUE)
), by=.(state, date, treated, g)]

# 5. Sun & Abraham event-study using fixest
cell[, rel_time := fifelse(treated==1, as.integer(year(date) - g), NA_integer_)]
# Create leads/lags from -10 to +10, omit -1
for (k in -10:10){
  if(k==-1) next
  cell[, paste0("D",k) := as.integer(rel_time==k)]
}

fml <- as.formula(paste(
  "temp_share ~",
  paste0("D", c(-10:-2,0:10), collapse=" + "),
  "+ unem + manuf + union | state + year(date)"
))

est_sa <- feols(fml, data=cell, cluster = ~state, sunab = ~g + year(date))
summary(est_sa)

# 6. Callaway & Sant’Anna ATT (state-year panel)
cell[, year := year(date)]
panel <- unique(cell, by=c("state","year"))
att_gt <- att_gt(yname="temp_share",
                 tname="year",
                 idname="state",
                 gname="g",
                 xformla= ~unem+manuf+union,
                 data=panel)
agg_effects <- aggte(att_gt, type="dynamic")
summary(agg_effects)

# 7. Robustness: use QCEW state-quarter data
# (Assume qcew.csv: state, date, temp_emp, total_emp, controls)
qcew <- fread("qcew.csv")
qcew <- merge(qcew, wd_implied, by="state", all.x=TRUE)
qcew[, treated := (!is.na(adopt_date) & date >= adopt_date)]
qcew[, share := temp_emp/total_emp]

robust <- feols(share ~ sunab(g, quarter(date)) + unem + manuf + union |
                 state + quarter(date), cluster = ~state, data=qcew)
summary(robust)
```

6. Expected Results
   Direction: Positive—adoption of wrongful-discharge protections raises firms’ reliance on temp agencies.  
   Magnitude: A one-doctrine adoption (implied-contract) is expected to increase temporary-help’s employment share by roughly 0.15–0.25 percentage points after 3–5 years (≈10–15 % of the 1995 mean). Stronger effects when all three doctrines are present (~0.4 pp).  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
   C1: Parallel trends supported by pre-trend tests ………………… 1  
   C2: No anticipation (leads near zero) ……………………………… 0.5  
   C3: No spillovers/interference ………………………………………… 0.5  
   C4: Stable composition of outcome and sample ………………… 1  
   C5: Exogenous policy timing conditional on controls ………… 0.5  
   Total ≈ 3.5 / 5 – credible but not bulletproof; robustness and falsification exercises are essential.
